intro: How can we reduce an observation to one of a few hard labels while retaining information about model parameters? We study this problem in score space—the space of local log-likelihood gradients—distinguishing labels for a fixed sample from a rule that can label future observations.

central.title: Stable D-optimal partitions have a geometric rule.
central.summary: If no allowed single-atom move improves the determinant of the retained information, every atom lies strictly nearest to its own cell centre in the metric defined by that information.
central.significance: A finite assignment therefore determines a reusable nearest-centre rule without another fit. This is the main structural bridge between optimizing labels and constructing a quantizer; it does not say that every stable partition is globally optimal.
central.qualification: The theorem requires merged duplicate atoms, positive-definite retained information, exactly K nonempty cells, and exact exchange stability over every move that keeps cells nonempty. Numerical stopping tolerances need their own certification.

results.title: Score each move exactly
results.summary: A closed-form determinant gain makes individual relocations comparable without refactorizing the information matrix.
results.significance: Accepting only strictly improving moves gives a monotone search that terminates on a finite sample.
results.qualification: The determinant identity is classical; its application to the coupled cell-centroid update is the adaptation here.

results.title: Global D optima are geometric
results.summary: Every finite global D optimum satisfies the same nearest-centre geometry under the structural theorem’s hypotheses.
results.significance: Searching for geometric rules need not lose the finite global optimum in this setting.
results.qualification: This is a consequence of the stability theorem, not an efficient algorithm for finding that optimum.

results.title: Bracket the profiled optimum
results.summary: For one parameter of interest, dynamic programming on a tilted scalar score supplies an achieved value and an upper bound.
results.significance: An exhibited closing labelling certifies a finite global profiled optimum.
results.qualification: Closure requires the stated saddle condition; a reported bracket alone is not an optimality certificate.

boundaries.title: Nuisance profiling can break the rule
boundaries.summary: An exact finite example has a global profiled optimum that violates its own first-order geometric rule.
boundaries.significance: The D theorem cannot simply be transferred to nuisance-adjusted information.
boundaries.qualification: A finite optimum alone does not authorize that geometric compilation.

boundaries.title: The certificate need not close
boundaries.summary: Exact examples show a genuine gap between the profiled primal optimum and its tilt dual.
boundaries.significance: A useful upper bound can remain strictly above the best attainable partition.
boundaries.qualification: The contribution is the explicit witnesses; minimax failure on a finite nonconvex problem is not itself new.

questions.title: Does finite optimality survive the population limit?
questions.summary: Restricted consistency is known. Can unrestricted empirical global D optima converge without the imposed margins?
questions.significance: This would connect exact finite optimization to population design.

questions.title: Which criteria force geometry?
questions.summary: D admits an exchange-to-geometry theorem; other familiar criteria have counterexamples.
questions.significance: A characterization would explain the structural distinction.
questions.qualification: Uniqueness of the determinant is not established.

questions.title: How robust is the rule to estimated scores?
questions.summary: Can score error control changes in retained information and cell boundaries?
questions.significance: This would connect learned representations to quantization guarantees.
questions.qualification: Proxy information is not automatically true Fisher information.
